Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30

Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Rios (Redwood SE), Evelyn Cho (CTO, Juno Labs), Samir Patel (Infra), Lena Roth (ML Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Juno Labs is evaluating Redwood for latency-sensitive inference with large variance in traffic. Main concerns: burst headroom, KV cache warmup, reserved GPU sizing, and warmup/eviction policies in a VPC/on-prem topology. Discussed queueing models (M/M/c vs deterministic bursts), probabilistic headroom, pre-warm strategies, and potential POC next steps.

Topics: capacity planning, burst policies, KV cache warmup, batching tradeoffs, quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem considerations, pilot scoping.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE on the infra team, and Carlos will lead the technical deep dive.
[00:12] Evelyn (CTO): Hi, Evelyn here. Thanks, excited to dig in. We want to validate burst resiliency for our chat product.
[00:18] Carlos (SE): Great—quick note on agenda: we'll go over your traffic shape, queuing models we recommend for burst safety, KV cache warmup strategies, then sizing reserved GPUs with probabilistic headroom.
[00:29] Samir (Infra): Sounds good. We have a lot of spiky traffic, some cron-driven batches. Main ask: keep p95/p99 under control without overcommitting GPUs.

[01:02] Carlos (SE): Right. Can you describe arrival patterns? Is it Poisson-ish or big scheduled spikes?
[01:10] Samir (Infra): Mostly Poisson for normal usage but we get periodic scheduled pushes — think 10x spikes for a few minutes, maybe once an hour. Also, nightly reindex jobs.
[01:22] Carlos (SE): Okay, that's the classic mixed-mode. For mixed Poisson plus deterministic spikes we model as compound arrival process. In practice we recommend two levers: reserved capacity sized for baseline plus predictive headroom, and a burst policy that can temporarily scale or route to less expensive variants.

[01:49] Maya (AE): Wanted to flag cost sensitivity — Juno's FP is sensitive to monthly committed spend, so reserved GPUs are attractive but need to be sized carefully.

[02:05] Lena (ML): Also the KV cache matters — our few-shot prompts mean cache hit rate is high, but cold starts cause token spikes and higher latency.

[02:18] Carlos (SE): Right. KV cache warmup often beats raw GPU spin-up time for user-perceived latency. We discussed 'snooze' or 'snoozing' pools — short-lived pre-warmed workers that keep KV warm without full reservation.

[02:35] Evelyn (CTO): Can you explain the snooze concept? We haven't heard that term before.

[02:42] Carlos (SE): Sure. 'Snooze' here means a small number of reserved or cheaper instances that we keep with lightweight state — enough to keep KV and prefix caches warm but not full-capacity GPU compute. When a spike hits, they'll absorb initial traffic and maintain low p95 while the main pools autoscale. Think of it as a warm buffer.

[03:08] Samir (Infra): How do we decide the snooze size? Is there a formula?

[03:15] Carlos (SE): We use a probabilistic model. Given your baseline lambda (requests/sec) and spike distribution (peak multiplier and duration), we compute required warm buffer W so that the probability of overload during the initial t_refill seconds is below a threshold. It's analogous to the M/M/c queue with time-varying arrival rate.

[03:38] Carlos (SE): Example: if baseline is 50 rps and spikes to 500 rps for ~120s, and your refill time (time to spin up extra GPUs) is ~90s, you'd compute W to handle the excess arrivals during that 90s with desired tail probability, say 0.01 for p99.

[04:01] Maya (AE): We actually made a sample sheet that shows different refills and required warm capacities. I'll send that after.

[04:08] Evelyn (CTO): That would be helpful. Also, we're running quantized models in prod — does quantization affect warmup behavior?

[04:17] Carlos (SE): Quantization reduces memory and can speed token throughput but has two side effects for warmup: 1) smaller KV entries (so cache warms faster per GB), 2) inference per-token time can change so refill time estimates need recalibration. We recommend running a micro-benchmark of cold vs warmed for your quant profile.

[04:40] Samir (Infra): We use int8 on A100s and sometimes int4 on T4s for cheaper bursts. Can Redwood route between quantized variants?

[04:49] Maya (AE): Yes, smart routing can fallback to quantized variants when cost or capacity constraints require. You can express a policy like 'prefer full-precision on reserved pool, fallback to int8 for burst overflow'.

[05:02] Carlos (SE): Routing also ties into KV coherence — when you route to a quantized variant, ensure your prefix cache keys are compatible, we version keys on model-variant to avoid cache poisoning.

[05:21] Lena (ML): About batching — aggressive batching increases throughput but worsens tail latency during spikes. How do we balance that?

[05:30] Carlos (SE): We recommend adaptive batching parameters: keep small max_batch during detected spikes and increase for stable periods. Our runtime supports continuous batching that adapts based on queue length and latency SLO. For Juno, we suggest a max latency SLO and set batcher to optimize for cost until queue exceeds threshold, then prioritize latency.

[05:58] Evelyn (CTO): So is this automatic or manual tuning?

[06:03] Carlos (SE): Both. Redwood Optimize can recommend initial settings; runtime will auto-adjust within safe bounds. You retain overrides if you want manual control.

[06:18] Samir (Infra): One big ask: we can't have cold VPC connections adding 200-300ms. Our infra is VPC-onprem hybrid. Any network suggestions?

[06:28] Carlos (SE): For VPC/private deployments we suggest persistent keepalive tunnels and NAT warmers. Also preflight warmup requests from inside the VPC to maintain TLS/connection state. For on-prem packages, we ship a lightweight agent to maintain that warm state.

[06:49] Maya (AE): Let's pivot to queueing model math — can you walk through the M/M/c vs time-varying model you mentioned?

[06:55] Carlos (SE): Sure. M/M/c assumes exponential inter-arrivals and service times and static c servers. For time-varying spikes, we use non-stationary queuing approximation. Practically we compute the expected number of arrivals during refill window T_refill and size warm buffer W so that the overflow probability P(N_arrivals > W + c_baseline * T_refill) < alpha. It's approximate but gives conservative sizing.

[07:30] Lena (ML): Is the refill time dominated by GPU provision or KV population?

[07:36] Carlos (SE): Depends on model. For our runtime, GPU provisioning (if using cloud ephemeral) can be 30-90 seconds. KV repopulation depends on your cache warmup strategy — if you use prefix prefetch or synthetic warmup queries you can reduce effective warm time to a few seconds.

[07:56] Samir (Infra): We can run synthetic warmup — curious about how many queries to heat the KV.

[08:02] Carlos (SE): Number scales with unique prefix diversity. If you have 10k popular prefixes, a targeted warmup of top 10% can produce high hit rates. We include a sample script that replays highest-frequency prefixes across the warm pool. That often gets you 70-90% of steady-state hit rate in <30s.

[08:27] Evelyn (CTO): Ok, so we could keep a small warm snooze pool and run continuous synthetic warmup during spikes to keep KV hot. But what about eviction policies — LRU vs TTL?

[08:37] Carlos (SE): LRU is default but in burst scenarios TTL-based retention for 'hot prefixes' can be better. Redwood supports pinned keys and hot-lists so you can mark critical prefixes to never evict for the duration of a campaign. For cost control we recommend a hybrid: pinned hotlist + LRU fallback.

[08:58] Maya (AE): Any risks around cache inconsistency across model variants?

[09:03] Carlos (SE): Only if you share keys across incompatible model variants. Version your keys by model+quant+tokenizer version. That avoids subtle correctness issues.

[09:16] Samir (Infra): Let's talk numbers. If we commit to 8 reserved GPUs for baseline, how much warmheadroom should we commit for 10x spikes?

[09:26] Carlos (SE): Rough rule: reserved baseline handles average throughput Buffer_B. For 10x spikes, you don't need 80 GPUs — you size W to cover arrivals during T_refill. Using our spreadsheet, for T_refill=90s and spike magnitude 10x (say baseline 200 rps->2000 rps), the warm buffer might be equivalent to 4-6 GPUs handling initial 90s; then autoscale fills the rest. So reserved 8 + snooze 4 could be good. But that's sensitive to your per-token latency and batching.

[09:57] Evelyn (CTO): That sounds promising. How about preemptible/spot instances? We are cost-conscious and can tolerate occasional preempts if we have redundancy.

[10:07] Carlos (SE): Preemptible instances work if you combine them with reserved capacity and admission control: critical requests go to reserved pool, opportunistic workloads use spot. We also recommend replication across preemptible pools and persistent queues that get drained gracefully. Redwood has strategies for graceful eviction and state checkpointing to handle preemption without user-visible errors.

[10:33] Samir (Infra): For on-prem, any special considerations for sizing?

[10:38] Carlos (SE): On-prem you control hardware so you can optimize for memory and NVLink bandwidth. Warmup and KV locality become more predictable, but you'll want to over-provision NIC buffers and local KV capacity to avoid network saturation during spikes. Also ensure your scheduler can prioritize warmup traffic.

[10:59] Maya (AE): We haven't discussed telemetry — what traces/logs will we get to validate SLOs?

[11:05] Carlos (SE): Redwood provides token-level latency traces, per-route request histograms, KV hit rates, cache population timelines, and scaling events. We'll also provide a playback simulator so you can run your traffic trace and see modeled latency under different policies.

[11:25] Lena (ML): Can we get the simulator to run stochastic arrivals?

[11:29] Carlos (SE): Yes — the simulator supports user-supplied arrival distributions: Poisson, bursty compound processes, and replay traces. It models batching, KV hit/miss penalty, and refill delays. It's not a perfect replica of the runtime but is useful for sizing decisions.

[11:48] Samir (Infra): Regarding security and VPC — if we run private deployment inside our VPC, how do we handle KMS and logs?

[11:57] Maya (AE): For Private we support customer-managed KMS and on-prem HSM in some configs. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via secure forwarders. We also support SAML SSO and RBAC for operator access.

[12:13] Evelyn (CTO): Great. Any compliance blockers for us? We operate in EU + US, need data residency controls.

[12:21] Carlos (SE): We can pin some regions to EU-hosted capacity or run Private deployment in EU data centers. Data residency is a common pattern. We'll share our compliance docs.

[12:33] Maya (AE): Back to sizing: do you recommend a canary for pilot?

[12:38] Carlos (SE): Yes — start with a canary that mirrors production traffic for a subset of users. Use traffic shaping to send 1-5% of traffic including spike windows to the Redwood pilot and validate tail latency and cache behavior. The playback simulator plus a 2-week canary is a good next step.

[12:58] Samir (Infra): What thresholds should we watch in the canary?

[13:03] Carlos (SE): Key metrics: p95/p99 latency, KV hit rate, cold-start rate (requests that hit un-warmed pools), and autoscale fill time. If p99 exceeds your SLO more than X% of windows, adjust warm buffer or reduce batch sizes.

[13:20] Maya (AE): Also we'll track cost per 1M tokens and per-request for burst periods.

[13:26] Evelyn (CTO): One more question: if we use prewarm 'snooze' machines, what's the incremental cost? We need a cap.

[13:34] Maya (AE): Snooze instances are smaller and can be charged differently; we usually model them as a small recurring cost vs the potential outage/reduced UX cost. We'll include cost models in the spreadsheet.

[13:48] Carlos (SE): Also note you can schedule snooze only during high-risk windows to save cost — e.g., keep it on during business hours and let it sleep at night. But that requires good predictive signals.

[14:03] Lena (ML): On predictive signals — can we use telemetry anomalies to preemptively scale?

[14:08] Carlos (SE): Yes — Redwood can ingest your anomaly stream and pre-warm pools based on early indicators. We also support webhook triggers from your orchestration layer. That's part of the advanced policy set.

[14:24] Samir (Infra): We have an ML model that predicts spikes ~30s in advance with reasonable precision — could integrate that?

[14:30] Carlos (SE): Perfect fit — you can push prewarm triggers to Redwood's control plane. That reduces required warm buffer and cost. We'll demo integration patterns in the POC.

[14:43] Evelyn (CTO): Any gotchas with logs or debugging when we have multiple model variants?

[14:48] Carlos (SE): Tag requests with model-variant IDs in traces. We also recommend per-variant dashboards to avoid mixing metrics.

[15:00] Maya (AE): Quick note: competitors — you mentioned SageMaker earlier. They offer similar scaling but not the same KV-first warmup tooling, right?

[15:08] Carlos (SE): Correct. SageMaker has autoscaling but less specialized KV-level prefix caching and prewarm runbooks integrated. Anthropic and some other vendors focus on model quality but not runtime-level warmup controls.

[15:22] Samir (Infra): Going back to the simulator — can it output expected costs for different policies?

[15:28] Carlos (SE): Yes — it has a cost model: tokens/sec * time * instance cost plus reserved commitments and snooze costs. We'll parameterize your actual pricing and simulate monthly spend.

[15:44] Lena (ML): For the POC, what's the minimum baseline to make the tests meaningful?

[15:49] Carlos (SE): For warmup/eviction validation, you need enough baseline traffic to get representative cache distributions — roughly 1-2k requests across a 24-hour sample. But for burst resilience tests, we'd replay your peak windows directly. Ideally provide 7-day traces.

[16:10] Maya (AE): We'll capture that as an action item.

[16:15] Evelyn (CTO): On the pilot timeline — what's realistic? We prefer to run this next month.

[16:20] Maya (AE): If Juno can provide traces and a primary contact for infra, we can spin up a pilot in 2-3 weeks and run an initial canary for 2 weeks.

[16:29] Samir (Infra): That works. One last deep technical question — when you do autoscale, how do you avoid thundering herd on KV repopulation?

[16:38] Carlos (SE): We have three defenses: 1) staggered join: new workers join in waves and request warm prefixes in prioritized order; 2) synthetic warmup traffic generated internally to pre-populate top-k prefixes; 3) admission control that limits inflight requests per new worker until warm threshold reached. Combined those avoid a full-scale repopulation storm.

[16:59] Lena (ML): Do we get hooks to change warm lists on the fly?

[17:04] Carlos (SE): Yes — you can update pinned hotlists via API and the runtime will adjust eviction accordingly.

[17:12] Maya (AE): Let's talk risks: what are common failure modes we should watch for?

[17:16] Carlos (SE): Common modes: mis-sized warm buffer (underprovisioning), not accounting for increased per-token time due to quant variance, and network cold starts in VPCs. Many of these are avoided with the playback sim and a short canary.

[17:33] Samir (Infra): Could you summarize recommended initial configuration for us?

[17:37] Carlos (SE): Sure: 1) Reserved baseline: 8 GPUs (matches your current baseline), 2) Snooze warm buffer: equivalent of 3-5 GPU workers depending on refill; keep snooze on business hours initially, 3) Enable synthetic warmup scripts pointed at top-5k prefixes, 4) Adaptive batching default with max latency bound 300-400ms, 5) Use int8 for opportunistic pools and full-precision for reserved, 6) Integrate predictive prewarm webhook if your spike predictor is reliable.

[18:12] Evelyn (CTO): That gives us a concrete plan. Let's talk measurements for success.

[18:17] Carlos (SE): Success criteria from Redwood side: p95 < 250ms and p99 < 600ms for in-SLO traffic, KV hit rate > 80% during spikes, and cost delta within agreed budget (we'll model). From Juno: maintain UX quality with <1% error rate and acceptable cost. We'll make exact thresholds part of the pilot agreement.

[18:42] Maya (AE): A couple of administrative items — we'll need an NDA addendum for trace sharing, and we'll put in a CR ID into your deal record.

[18:54] Samir (Infra): We'll route traces via secure S3 bucket with encryption.

[19:00] Carlos (SE): Good. For the POC we will also provide the simulator, runbook, and sample prewarm scripts.

[19:08] Evelyn (CTO): Anything else on on-prem network tuning?

[19:12] Carlos (SE): Tune TCP keepalives, increase socket buffers, and ensure your NAT gateway capacity is sufficient. We'll provide a checklist.

[19:24] Maya (AE): Ok, wrapping up — quick recap and next steps.

[19:28] Maya (AE): Action items: Maya send pricing and simulation sheet; Carlos send runbook and sample scripts; Juno to provide traces and confirm pilot contacts. We'll schedule pilot kickoff for week of Apr 13 pending deliverables.

[19:44] Evelyn (CTO): Thanks, everyone. This was productive.
[19:48] Samir (Infra): Thanks.
[19:49] Lena (ML): Thanks.

[20:00] End of recording.
